message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing by telling people there's no end credits scene in the movie. Let me start by understanding the situation. I work as an usher at a movie theater, and my job is to clean the theaters after the movie ends. I was cleaning two theaters at the same time, one showing Dark Phoenix and another movie that was pretty crowded. When I walked into Dark Phoenix, the credits were rolling, and there were four sets of people still there, probably waiting for an end credits scene, which is common in superhero movies. I thought, "Hey, I can help them out by telling them there's no end credits scene. That way, they can leave faster, and I can clean the theater quicker too." So I told them, "Hey guys, you don't have to wait around, there's no end credits scene." I've done this before without any issues, but this time, a couple got upset. They yelled at me for ruining their movie experience and wanted to speak to a manager. I called the manager, and they told the couple that I was rude for spoiling the information and that I was shining a flashlight, which I denied. I told my manager that I didn't see an issue with telling them because it saved time. The manager apologized to the couple and gave them a free movie pass. After they left, the manager told me to stop telling people about the absence of end credits scenes. Now, I'm wondering if I did the right thing or if this was just a weird couple. I need to consider a few factors here. First, my intention was to help both the customers and myself. By informing them, I thought I was being efficient and considerate. However, the couple took it negatively, which made me question my approach. I should think about the customers' perspective. Some people might appreciate the heads-up to save time, especially if they're in a hurry. But others might feel that knowing there's no end credits scene ruins their experience, especially if they're expecting a bonus scene. It's possible that the couple felt disappointed because they were looking forward to something that wasn't there, and I took that away from them. Another point is the theater's policy. My manager told me to stop doing this, which suggests that the theater doesn't want us to inform customers about the absence of end credits scenes. Maybe they believe it's not our place to comment on the movie content, or perhaps they want to avoid any potential conflicts with customers. I also need to consider the practical aspects. By telling people there's no end credits scene, I can clean the theater faster, which is efficient. But if it leads to complaints, it might not be worth it. The manager's decision to give the couple a free pass indicates that they value customer satisfaction over efficiency in this case. I should also reflect on how I delivered the message. Maybe the way I told them came off as rude or dismissive. If I had phrased it differently, perhaps they wouldn't have reacted so negatively. For example, instead of saying, "You don't have to wait," I could have said, "Just a heads-up, there's no end credits scene, so you can leave whenever you're ready." That might have been more polite and less intrusive. Additionally, I should think about the broader implications. If I continue to inform people, I might face more complaints, which could affect my job performance. On the other hand, if I stop, I might be less efficient, but I can avoid potential conflicts. In conclusion, while my intention was to be helpful, the way I approached the situation might have been the issue. The couple's reaction, along with the manager's instruction, suggests that it's better to avoid telling customers about the absence of end credits scenes to maintain customer satisfaction and avoid conflicts.
